set.notes: Walker 2003 (PMID:14596323) compared citrate, an amino-acid chelate, oxide and placebo in 46 healthy participants at 300 mg/day for 60 days. Citrate had favorable serum/saliva results and organic preparations outperformed oxide on urinary measures. This does not establish a universal exact glycinate-versus-citrate ranking. Firoz 2001 (PMID:11794633) did not test citrate; it compared oxide with chloride, lactate and aspartate. Sean approved a tied top score of 15 for citrate, chloride, lactate and aspartate on 2026-10-13: cross-study evidence supports the top group, not an order within it.

A natural magnesium salt from seawater (brand: Ancient Minerals). Well-absorbed orally. Also popular as 'magnesium oil' for transdermal application (topical absorption is debated but widely used for muscle cramps and relaxation). One of the few forms available for both oral and topical use. Evidence update 2026-04-25 (Batch 15): Magnesium audit — 11 PMIDs WebFetch-verified. CLASS FINDING: organic chelates (glycinate, malate, taurate, orotate, AAC, gluconate, aspartate, lactate, chloride) cluster F ~25-45% in humans with overlapping CIs; only robustly-replicated human ranking is citrate ≥ organic chelates > carbonate > oxide. THREONATE FINDING: BBB-crossing claim is RAT-ONLY (Slutsky 2010 PMID:20152124, Neuron). Liu 2016 + Zhang 2022 human cognitive RCTs have NO brain Mg PK. ACETYL-TAURATE: rodent-only (Ates 2019 mice, Uysal 2019 rats); no human PK. BROWN RICE CHELATE: re-confirmed 0 PubMed hits (Batch 11). Misattributions caught: Slutsky PMID 20152120→20152124; Walker 2003 did NOT test glycinate; Schwalfenberg 2017 muscle-cramps RCT does not exist; Coudray PMID 16253138→16548135. Clinician recalibration 2026-06-02: bio_score is absorption/bioavailability only; natural/source and tolerability claims are not counted in bio_score. API evidence trail: scripts/audits/mineral_forms_20260602/api_verification.json. Sean approved a tied top score of 15 for citrate, chloride, lactate and aspartate on 2026-10-13: cross-study evidence supports the top group, not an order within it.

form_evidence.rationale: A direct human comparison found magnesium chloride more bioavailable than magnesium oxide and comparable with the other well-absorbed salts tested. A small randomized crossover in 12 healthy adults also found chloride solution raised 24-hour urinary magnesium, with overall blood effects similar to gluconate and slow-release chloride.

Schuette 1994 (PMID:7815675) compared 100 mg isotope-labeled magnesium diglycinate with oxide in 12 ileal-resection patients. Overall absorption did not differ (23.5% versus 22.8%); a four-patient subgroup with poor oxide absorption benefited and diglycinate was better tolerated. This does not establish superiority or inferiority versus citrate in healthy adults. Walker 2003 (PMID:14596323) tested an amino-acid chelate; its abstract does not identify that preparation as exact glycinate. Sean's 2026-10-13 calibration kept bio_score 12 because direct human evidence is mixed and does not place it in the tied top tier; tolerability and absorption are distinct outcomes.

form_evidence.rationale: Graded moderate under the existing rubric: direct human absorption studies of the named glycine chelate with comparators, whose results are mixed. A randomized crossover isotope study gave 100 mg diglycinate or oxide to 12 patients after ileal resection: overall absorption was equal (23.5% vs 22.8%); the four poorest oxide absorbers absorbed more from diglycinate, with an earlier peak, a larger isotope AUC and better tolerance. Two industry-funded single-dose crossovers in healthy adults compared bisglycinate with citrate and oxide (one gave 375 mg magnesium as orosoluble powders; one gave 350 mg commercial preparations): one found no significant AUC difference among the tested sources, and neither showed bisglycinate superiority. These findings support 12, not the top tier, and do not extend to buffered, lysinate-glycinate or unspecified amino-acid chelate preparations.

form_evidence.rationale: EFSA's 2024 opinion concluded magnesium is bioavailable from magnesium L-threonate and that the source is not nutritionally disadvantageous, based on a dissociation study, two rat studies and one human trial. It did not compare it with other magnesium salts, so 11 is a calibrated placement matching citrate-malate, not a measured rank. Cognitive claims are assessed separately from bio_score.

form_evidence.rationale: A randomized crossover in 12 healthy adults compared magnesium gluconate tablets with magnesium chloride solution and slow-release chloride at 16 mmol. Overall serum, ultrafiltrable and leukocyte magnesium effects showed no major differences; only the chloride solution significantly raised 24-hour urinary magnesium over baseline. One small study does not establish a higher comparative tier, so the score stays 10.
